summary: Both taxi runs read as credible owner-driver accounts: fares, fuel, road tax/insurance, repairs and admin costs all appear at sensible scale for a 12-month period, capitalised vehicle spend is excluded from the P&L as the product intends, and the self-assessment and tax figures follow from the reported profit. The only points worth a human glance are the second scenario's £200 capitalised asset carrying no capital allowance and its blank Fixed Assets cost cell; neither blocks the run.

concerns.figure: Fixed Assets: New Asset Cost blank (—) while Purchase Analysis shows Vehicle purchases capitalised 200
concerns.where: taxi-scenario-sp-sixty, Fixed Assets section (no D47 row in appendix) vs PurchasesMar T1
concerns.why: The £200 of code-f capital spend reaches the Purchases sheet's fixed asset column but no cost appears on the Fixed Assets schedule, and Total WDA/AIA are both zero, so the asset attracts no capital allowance at all. Worth confirming the schedule is meant to leave a small addition unrecorded rather than dropping it.

concerns.figure: Capital Allowances 0 and Mileage Allowance 0 together
concerns.where: taxi-scenario-sp-sixty, Profit & Loss Account B10 and B11
concerns.why: The scenario says the sheet takes actual running costs with capital allowances or the mileage allowance, whichever gives the lower profit; here actual costs are taken but the capital allowance line is nil because the only addition (£200) generated no allowance. Self-consistent, but a reader may expect some allowance against a capitalised purchase.
